recommended: EU 2012 tolerance table (European Commission guidance for competent authorities, Dec 2012) for every food macronutrient, counted one-sided, i.e. only in the direction that hurts the buyer (FDA 21 CFR 101.9(g) logic and EU guidance s.2.3). FDA's 120% rule for energy, which the EU table does not cover. FSSAI's legal -10% rules shown alongside: as the scoring rule for supplements (Nutra Regs 2016 reg 3(11)), and as an extra 'below India's legal tolerance' flag for protein/fibre shortfalls in ordinary foods. Penalty scales with deviation in multiples of the tolerance band: 0 at <=1x, rising to the maximum at >=3x.
why: 1) FSSAI's general rule exists but cannot carry the score alone. FSS (Labelling & Display) Regs 2020 reg 5(3)(d), as published in the Version VIII compendium (09.09.2025), reads 'tolerance of maximum minus 10 percent of the value for that nutrient declared on the label at any point in time within declared shelf life'. It is one flat percentage with no absolute band. Read literally, it only limits shortfalls and says nothing about extra sugar, sodium or fat. It does not say whether measurement uncertainty is included. It is also contested: a 22.10.2021 Direction kept the 'status quo / established practices' on tolerance, a ±20% replacement was run by s.16(5) Directions from 1.7.2022 to 30.6.2024, and the 30.08.2024 Direction re-operationalised the 2022 amendments EXCEPT the tolerance provision. Final notification is still pending. 2) The EU 2012 table is the most complete official, numeric, per-nutrient scheme. Absolute bands at low amounts (±2 g sugars/protein/fibre below 10 g, ±1.5 g fat, ±0.8 g sat fat, ±0.15 g sodium) avoid false 'dishonest' verdicts on small numbers, where 10% is below lab precision. The values explicitly INCLUDE measurement uncertainty, so a lab value can be compared directly with no extra allowance. That suits OpenLabel, which usually tests one or a few units, not a 12-unit composite like the FDA. 3) Direction: FDA 101.9(g)(4)-(6) makes the asymmetry law. Protein, fibre and similar must be >=80% of label (Class II, naturally occurring) or >=100% (Class I, added). Calories, sugars, added sugars, total/sat/trans fat, cholesterol and sodium must be <=120%. Excess of the first group and shortfall of the second are 'reasonable' under GMP. EU guidance s.2.3 states the same consumer-interest logic for fats, sugars and salt vs nutrients 'where consumers are generally interested in higher levels'. Codex CAC/GL 2-1985 s.3.5 sets no numbers and leaves tolerances to be set by competent authorities, with public health concerns as one criterion. 4) Energy: the EU table has no energy row. FDA's '<=120% of declared calories' is the only official numeric rule, so we use it. 5) Supplements: India has a specific primary rule, Nutra Regs 2016 reg 3(11): 'not more than (-) ten per cent from the declared value of the nutrients or nutritional ingredients'. It is stricter than the EU's -20%, covers non-vitamin actives too, and applies at analysis of the finished product, so it should drive the shortfall score for multivitamins and protein powders licensed as health supplements. On the high side, India sets only manufacturing overage caps (Schedule I Table C) and RDA-based maxima, so excess is better treated as a safety issue than an honesty one.

energy_kcal.source: FDA 21 CFR 101.9(g)(5): calories must not exceed 120% of label (no action if the excess is within the method's recognised analytical variability). The EU 2012 table has no energy row.
energy_kcal.note: Optional OpenLabel-only floor (NOT official): treat tolerance as max(20% of declared, 10 kcal/100 g) so near-zero-calorie drinks are not flagged over 1-2 kcal. Better still, compute energy from lab macros using FSSAI reg 5(3)(e) factors (carb 4, protein 4, fat 9, fibre 2 kcal/g) and score the macros, not the energy.

protein_g.source: EU 2012 Table 1 (carbohydrate, sugars, protein, fibre). Direction from FDA 101.9(g)(4) (protein >=80% Class II / 100% Class I) and EU s.2.3. Show an FSSAI L&D reg 5(3)(d) (-10%) flag alongside; for protein_powder licensed as a health supplement, score with Nutra reg 3(11) -10% instead.

fat_g.source: EU 2012 Table 1 (fat). Direction from FDA 101.9(g)(5) (total fat <=120%).

sugars_g.source: EU 2012 Table 1 (sugars). Direction from FDA 101.9(g)(5) (total sugars <=120%).

added_sugars_g.source: No regime sets an analytical tolerance for added sugars alone. The EU has no added-sugars declaration, so the sugars band is borrowed. FDA 101.9(g)(5) applies the 120% rule to added sugars ONLY when the food's only sugars are added sugars; otherwise compliance is by manufacturer records (101.9(g)(10)).
added_sugars_g.note: A lab cannot measure added sugars, only total sugars. Score added sugars only when lab total sugars exceed the declared ADDED sugars beyond this band AND the product has no intrinsic sugars (no milk, fruit, etc.). Otherwise compare lab total sugars with declared sugars_g and skip added_sugars_g.

fiber_g.source: EU 2012 Table 1 (fibre). Direction from FDA 101.9(g)(4) (dietary fibre >=80% Class II / 100% Class I). Show an FSSAI L&D -10% flag alongside.

sodium_mg.source: EU 2012 Table 1 (sodium: <0.5 g/100 g ±0.15 g; >=0.5 g/100 g ±20%), converted to mg. Direction from FDA 101.9(g)(5) (sodium <=120%).
sodium_mg.note: The EU table drops from 150 mg to 100 mg at 500 mg declared (20% of 500). To avoid the cliff, implement as max(150, 20%).

vitamins_minerals.under_source: FSSAI Nutra Regs 2016 reg 3(11): variation at analysis of finished products 'shall not be more than (-) ten per cent from the declared value of the nutrients or nutritional ingredients on the label' (FSSAI FAQ Q25 confirms). Stricter than EU 2012 Table 2 (-20%) and FDA 101.36(f)/101.9(g)(4) (Class I added nutrients >=100%).

eu_2012_table2.note: EU upper tolerance including measurement uncertainty; higher accepted for vitamin C in liquids; capped by legal maximum amounts

over_reference.fssai_overage_note: Nutra Regs 2016 Schedule I Table C: the most a maker may add above label claim to cover shelf-life loss ('unless scientifically justified'; label must say 'appropriate overages added'). It is a manufacturing allowance, not an explicit analytical tolerance.

vitamins_minerals.recommendation: Score shortfall below -10% as dishonest (FSSAI). Report excess above declared+EU upper tolerance (+50% vitamins / +45% minerals) as an 'over-label' note. Route excess above RDA/upper limits to the SAFETY part, since both EU s.2.1 and FSSAI treat excess vitamins/minerals as a safety question.

other_actives.under_source: FSSAI Nutra Regs 2016 reg 3(11) covers 'nutrients or nutritional ingredients', so it applies to protein in health-supplement protein powders, amino acids, botanicals and other nutraceutical actives. FDA 101.36(f)(1) applies Class I/II criteria to other dietary ingredients. The EU sets no tolerance for non-vitamin/mineral actives.
other_actives.over_reference: No official upper analytical tolerance. FDA 101.36(f)(1): 'Reasonable excesses over labeled amounts are acceptable within current good manufacturing practice.'
other_actives.note: For protein_powder, also check amino-spiking (free glycine/taurine etc. inflating Kjeldahl N x 6.25) in the 'spiking' group. A powder that meets protein only through spiking should fail honesty.

severity_suggestion: Neither EU nor FDA grades how far a value is out of tolerance. EU s.2.4 says authorities should weigh 'the extent of the deviation', the nutrient and its direction, and FDA only says no action within method variability. So the scale is ours, anchored on the official band. Steps: (1) compute tol = band(declared) from the table above (optionally widen declared to its EU s.6 rounding bounds first); (2) deviation d = lab - declared for 'over' nutrients, declared - lab for 'under' nutrients; if d <= 0 there is no penalty (deviation in the harmless direction is never penalised, per FDA 101.9(g)(6)); (3) r = d / tol. r <= 1: within official tolerance, 0 penalty, status 'matches label'. 1 < r <= 2: 'off the label', penalty rising linearly from 0 to half the per-nutrient maximum. 2 < r <= 3: 'well off the label', penalty rising to the maximum. r > 3: maximum penalty. Worked examples: sugars declared 20 g (tol 4 g): lab 24 g = within; 28 g = r 2.0 (40% over); 32 g = r 3.0 (60% over), max. Sodium declared 300 mg (tol 150 mg): lab 450 = within, 600 = r 2.0. Because the EU bands already include measurement uncertainty, r <= 1 must never be called dishonest. Because OpenLabel tests one or a few units, not the FDA's 12-unit composite (101.9(g)(2)), cap the single-nutrient penalty and show 'single sample' wording until a repeat test confirms. Supplements use the same r scale with tol = 10% of declared (FSSAI).
fssai_position: General packaged food: FSS (Labelling & Display) Regs 2020 reg 5(3)(d) as published (compendium Version VIII, 09.09.2025): 'The compliance to quantity of declared nutrients on the label shall have the tolerance of maximum minus 10 percent of the value for that nutrient declared on the label at any point in time within declared shelf life of the product.' History: 22.10.2021 Direction kept the 'status quo' on tolerances (secondary source); the draft L&D Amendment Regs 2022 proposed '± 20 percent', operationalised by s.16(5) Directions of 17.06.2022, 06.01.2023, 17.10.2023 and 05.06.2024 (to 30.06.2024); the 30.08.2024 Direction re-operationalised the 2022 amendments from 01.07.2024 'except the provisions relating to tolerance limit i.e. compliance to quantity of declared nutrients on the label with tolerance of ± 20 percent', and the final amendment approved at the 43rd Food Authority meeting excludes the tolerance provision. So the published text is -10%, but FSSAI is still deciding. The rule is one-sided (shortfall), flat, and silent on measurement uncertainty and on extra sugar/sodium/fat. Food service establishments (reg 9(4)/ch.3 proviso): 'deviation of 25 percent may be tolerated in case of nutritional information declaration', which does not cover packaged food. Supplements/nutraceuticals: Nutra Regs 2016 reg 3(11), '(-) ten per cent' from declared value at analysis of finished products, plus Schedule I Table C overage caps. FSSAI publishes no EU-style absolute bands and no 'harmful direction' rule.
notes: 1) Codex CAC/GL 2-1985 s.3.5 gives NO numbers. It says tolerance limits 'should be set in relation to public health concerns, shelf-life, accuracy of analysis, processing variability and inherent lability and variability of the nutrient', and whether the nutrient is added or natural. Declared values should be weighted averages of representative analyses, and Codex commodity standards take precedence. The rule that 'beneficial nutrients must not fall below 80% and restricted ones must not exceed the label' is FDA 101.9(g), not Codex. 2) Shelf life: EU s.2.2 and FSSAI 5(3)(d) both apply the tolerance at any time during shelf life, so testing a retail pack before its best-before date is fair. 3) EU s.2.3: declared values should be averages, not set at the favourable edge of the band. A pattern of values sitting at the edge across repeat tests is itself a sign of gaming. 4) Nutrient or health claims (e.g. 'high protein', 'low sugar') get tighter, one-sided EU Table 3 tolerances (measurement uncertainty only on the claim side) and FSSAI claim thresholds. That is out of scope here, but worth adding: a 'high protein' pack at 80% of label is worse than an unclaimed one. 5) FDA compliance uses a composite of 12 consumer units from 12 random cases per lot (101.9(g)(2)); supplements use 12 units or 10% of the lot, whichever is smaller (101.36(f)(1)). 6) Trans fat: FDA puts it in the <=120% group, and FSSAI requires trans-fat declaration for fats/oils and foods containing them. If it is ever compared, reuse the saturated-fat band as an OpenLabel choice (EU has no trans-fat row). 7) Not verified: the current Codex 2021 PDF wording of s.3.5; the primary text of the 22.10.2021 'status quo' direction; any post-2021 Nutra amendment to reg 3(11); any FSSAI enforcement note on how -10% is read for restricted nutrients.
